everyday: In everyday speech a field is a piece of land or an area of study; in physics it is a quantity spread through space.

meanings.short: Something that has a value at every point of space, such as the temperature, the wind velocity or the electric field at each place.
meanings.long: A field fills space: at each point it has a size and often a direction. In physics fields carry forces: a charge or mass changes the space around it by making a field, and another body feels a force from the field where it is. Electric, magnetic and gravitational fields are the main examples.

meanings.short: In algebra, a number system such as the real or complex numbers, in which you can add, subtract, multiply and divide (except by zero).
meanings.long: The numbers a vector space is built over form a field. Taking the real numbers gives a real vector space and the complex numbers a complex one. This is unrelated to a physical field such as the electric field.

meanings.short: A description of nature in which forces travel from point to point through fields, at a finite speed, instead of jumping across empty space.
meanings.long: Classical electromagnetism was the first field theory: a charge makes a field, the field spreads out at the speed of light, and other charges respond to the field where they are. General relativity and the theories of particle physics are field theories too.

meanings.short: The theory that describes particles as small bundles of energy in fields that fill all of space, combining quantum mechanics with special relativity.
meanings.long: In quantum field theory every kind of particle, such as the electron or the photon, belongs to a field, and a particle is a quantum of that field. The standard model of particle physics is a quantum field theory; it also predicts an energy of empty space, the vacuum energy.

meanings.short: The old idea that bodies push or pull each other instantly across empty space, with nothing in between passing the force along.
meanings.long: Newton's gravity and Coulomb's electric force were first understood this way. Field theory replaced the idea: the force is carried by a field, point by point, and changes spread at a finite speed.

meanings.short: A quantity that has a single number, with no direction, at every point of space, such as the temperature in a room.
meanings.long: A scalar field gives one number at each point, and possibly at each time. Temperature, pressure and electric potential are examples. Its slope from place to place is described by the gradient, a vector field.

meanings.short: A field of particle physics with one number at each point of space, such as the field thought to have driven inflation.
meanings.long: In cosmology a scalar field is a physical substance filling space, like the inflaton or a possible dark energy field. Its energy depends on its value through a potential energy curve, and a field that changes slowly acts like a vacuum energy.

meanings.short: A field of particle physics with one number at each point of space, such as the field thought to have driven inflation.
A rule that attaches an arrow, with a size and a direction, to every point of space, such as the wind velocity at each place.
meanings.long: A vector field gives a vector at each point. The electric and magnetic fields, the gravitational field and the velocity of a flowing fluid are vector fields. They are drawn as arrows on a grid or as field lines.

meanings.short: Curves drawn so that at every point they run along the field; where they crowd together the field is strong.
meanings.long: Electric field lines start on positive charges and end on negative ones, and two lines never cross. The number of lines crossing a surface is a picture of the flux through it.

meanings.short: The pull of gravity at each point of space, given as the force on each kilogram of mass placed there.
meanings.long: The gravitational field of a mass M points towards it and has size GM/r² at distance r. A mass m placed in the field feels the force m times the field, so near the Earth's surface the field is the familiar g of about 9.8 newtons per kilogram.

meanings.short: The electric push or pull at each point of space, given as the force on each coulomb of charge placed there.
meanings.long: The electric field at a point is the force on a small positive test charge divided by its charge, so a charge q there feels the force qE. It points away from positive charges and towards negative ones, and is measured in newtons per coulomb, the same as volts per metre.

meanings.short: The field made by magnets and moving charges, which pushes sideways on other moving charges and turns compass needles.
meanings.long: A magnetic field B exerts a force on a charge q moving with velocity v equal to q times v crossed with B: at right angles to both the motion and the field. Currents make magnetic fields, by the Biot–Savart law. It is measured in tesla.

meanings.short: Coming only in whole-number multiples of a smallest amount, or in a set of separate allowed values, never anything in between.
meanings.long: Electric charge is quantized: every charge is a whole multiple of the electron's charge e. In quantum mechanics energy, angular momentum and other quantities are often quantized in the same sense.

everyday: In everyday speech energy means liveliness or fuel; in physics it is an exact, measured quantity.

meanings.short: A quantity, measured in joules, that a body or field has because of its motion, position or state; a closed system keeps its total.
meanings.long: Energy comes as kinetic energy of motion, potential energy of position, heat, light and the energy stored in electric and magnetic fields. In a closed system the total stays the same: energy is conserved. (In an expanding universe this needs care: a freely travelling photon loses energy as it is redshifted.)

meanings.short: The force pushing on a surface divided by the area of the surface, so the push on each square metre.
meanings.long: Pressure is force per unit area, measured in pascals (newtons per square metre). In a gas it comes from molecules hitting the walls; radiation has pressure too, because light carries momentum. In a fluid at rest it pushes equally in every direction.

meanings.short: A sideways push: neighbouring magnetic field lines behave as if they repel each other.
meanings.long: Field lines can be pictured as stretched elastic strings that also push sideways on each other. The sideways push is this page's pressure; the pull along each line is its tension.

meanings.short: The energy stored in each cubic metre of space, for example in an electric or magnetic field, or in radiation.
meanings.long: An electric field E stores the energy density ε₀E²/2 and a magnetic field B stores B²/2μ₀, in joules per cubic metre. In cosmology the energy density of matter, radiation and the vacuum decides how the universe expands.

meanings.short: How much energy a wave, or a beam of particles, carries each second through each square metre of a surface facing it.
meanings.long: For light and other waves, intensity is the energy arriving per second per square metre, averaged over a cycle, measured in watts per square metre. It grows as the square of the wave's amplitude, which is why interference patterns are worked out by adding fields first and squaring afterwards.

meanings.short: The equation waves obey: how sharply the disturbance curves in space sets how strongly each point accelerates, so shapes travel at a fixed speed.
meanings.long: In one dimension it says that the second derivative in time equals the speed squared times the second derivative in space. Any shape travelling at that speed, in either direction, solves it. Maxwell's equations give it for electric and magnetic fields, with the speed of light.

meanings.short: At right angles to the direction of travel; a transverse wave shakes across the direction it moves, as light and waves on a string do.
meanings.long: In a transverse wave the disturbance is across the direction of travel. In a light wave both the electric and the magnetic field are at right angles to the direction of travel and to each other. Sound in air is the opposite kind, longitudinal, shaking along the direction of travel.

meanings.short: The direction in which the electric field of a light wave (or other transverse wave) swings back and forth.
meanings.long: A wave is polarized when its electric field swings along one fixed line (linear polarization), or turns round in a circle or ellipse as it travels. Light from a bulb or the Sun mixes all directions and is unpolarized; an antenna sends out waves polarized along its rods.

meanings.short: The lining up of tiny electric dipoles inside a material by an electric field, measured as dipole moment per unit volume.
meanings.long: In a dielectric the field turns polar molecules and stretches non-polar ones, so the material gets many small aligned dipoles. Their effect is like a thin layer of charge on each surface, which weakens the field inside.

meanings.short: Of two oscillations or waves: rising and falling together, reaching their peaks at the same moments.
meanings.long: Two oscillations of the same frequency are in phase when their phase difference is zero (or a whole number of cycles). In a light wave travelling through empty space the electric and magnetic fields are in phase.

meanings.short: A point of a standing wave where nothing moves: the wave is always zero there.
meanings.long: In a standing wave each point oscillates with its own amplitude. At the nodes the amplitude is zero; neighbouring nodes are half a wavelength apart, with an antinode halfway between. The zeros of a quantum wavefunction inside its region are also called nodes.

meanings.short: A point of a graph, in the sense of a network of points joined by lines (edges).
meanings.long: In linear algebra a graph is a set of nodes and edges, each edge joining two nodes. An electrical network is an example: the nodes are the junctions and the edges are the wires.

meanings.short: An equilibrium point of a pair of differential equations where all nearby paths flow in, or all flow out, without circling round.
meanings.long: In a phase portrait a node has two real eigenvalues of the same sign: both negative gives a stable node, which every nearby path approaches, both positive an unstable one. A saddle has eigenvalues of opposite sign, and a spiral has complex ones.

meanings.short: An equilibrium point of a pair of differential equations where all nearby paths flow in, or all flow out, without circling round.
meanings.long: In a phase portrait a node has two real eigenvalues of the same sign: both negative gives a stable node, which every nearby path approaches, both positive an unstable one. A saddle has eigenvalues of opposite sign, and a spiral has complex ones.

meanings.short: A place where several filaments of the cosmic web meet; the richest galaxy clusters sit there.
Of an orbit: a point where it crosses the reference plane; the ascending node is where it crosses going upwards.
meanings.long: Two orbital nodes lie on the line where the orbit's plane cuts the reference plane. Together with the inclination they fix how the orbit's plane is tilted in space.

meanings.short: A point of a standing wave, halfway between two nodes, where the wave swings most strongly.
meanings.long: At an antinode the amplitude of a standing wave is largest, twice that of each of the two travelling waves that make it. Antinodes are half a wavelength apart.

meanings.short: What happens when waves overlap: they add, strengthening each other where crest meets crest and cancelling where crest meets trough.
meanings.long: Where two waves overlap, their fields add. When the difference in path is a whole number of wavelengths, the waves arrive in step and the result is bright (constructive interference); half a wavelength more, they cancel and it is dark (destructive interference).

origin: Latin diffringere, to break into pieces.

meanings.short: The spreading of a wave as it passes an edge or goes through an opening about as narrow as its wavelength.
meanings.long: When a wave passes a slit or an obstacle, parts of the wave front that travel different distances interfere, giving a pattern of bright and dark bands. The narrower the opening compared with the wavelength, the wider the spreading.

meanings.short: A plate with many evenly spaced slits or lines, which sends each colour of light off in its own sharp directions.
meanings.long: Light from all the slits interferes; the bright directions are those where neighbouring slits differ in path by a whole number of wavelengths. With many slits these bright lines are very sharp, so a grating separates colours precisely.

meanings.short: Of waves: keeping in step, with a fixed difference in timing (phase) between them, so that their interference pattern stays still.
meanings.long: Two sources are coherent when the difference between their phases does not change. Only then do bright and dark bands stay in place long enough to be seen. A laser is coherent; the light of an ordinary bulb is not.

origin: Greek monos, single, and chroma, colour.

meanings.short: Of light or another wave: having a single frequency, and so a single wavelength and, for light, a single colour.
meanings.long: A monochromatic wave has one wavelength. Interference patterns are sharp only for monochromatic light, because each wavelength puts its bright bands in different places.

meanings.short: The experiment in which light passing through two close, narrow slits makes bright and dark bands on a screen, showing that light is a wave.
meanings.long: Thomas Young's experiment of about 1801: light from the two slits interferes, giving bright bands where the paths differ by a whole number of wavelengths. The band spacing gives the wavelength of the light.

meanings.short: The rule that an obstacle and a hole of the same shape make the same diffraction pattern, apart from the straight-through beam.
meanings.long: The waves from an opening and from the complementary screen add up to the unobstructed wave. So away from the direct beam their diffraction patterns are the same: a thin wire diffracts like a slit of the same width.

meanings.short: A layer of material, such as a soap film or an oil slick, about as thick as a wavelength of light.
meanings.long: Light reflected from the top and bottom of a thin film interferes. Which colours are strengthened depends on the film's thickness, which gives soap bubbles and oil on water their bright colours.

meanings.short: The SI unit of electric charge: the charge carried past a point in one second by a current of one ampere.
meanings.long: One coulomb is a large charge: the electron's charge is about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs, so a coulomb is the charge of about 6 × 10¹⁸ electrons.

meanings.short: The amount of electric charge in each unit of length, area or volume, depending on how the charge is spread.
meanings.long: Charge spread along a line has a linear charge density (coulombs per metre), charge on a surface a surface charge density (coulombs per square metre), and charge filling a volume a volume charge density (coulombs per cubic metre).

meanings.short: Charge that can be moved about or placed on purpose, such as the charge on capacitor plates, as opposed to charge bound inside molecules.
meanings.long: In a dielectric the field shifts the bound charges of the molecules slightly. Gauss's law can be written with only the free charge, if the field is multiplied by the dielectric constant.

meanings.short: A pair of equal and opposite electric charges a small distance apart.
meanings.long: A dipole has no net charge, but its two charges do not quite cancel: far away its field falls as one over distance cubed. In a uniform field it feels a torque that turns it to line up with the field. Many molecules, such as water, are electric dipoles.

meanings.short: The strength and direction of a dipole: the charge times the separation, as an arrow from the negative to the positive charge.
meanings.long: For charges +q and −q a distance d apart the dipole moment has size qd and points from −q to +q. The dipole's far field, and the torque and energy in an outside field, depend only on this arrow.

meanings.short: A dipole seen from so far away, compared with the distance between its charges, that its size no longer matters.
meanings.long: Far from a dipole its field depends only on the dipole moment, not on the separate charges and distance. A point dipole is the limit in which the separation shrinks to nothing while the dipole moment stays fixed.

meanings.short: The field close to one of several charges, where that nearest charge dominates and the field lines point straight out from it.
meanings.long: When sketching the field of several charges, close to each charge its own field is much stronger than the others, so the lines there are nearly radial.

meanings.short: The field far from a group of charges, where it looks like that of one charge equal to their total, if that is not zero.
meanings.long: Seen from far away, a group of charges acts like a single charge equal to their sum. If the total is zero, the far field is that of a dipole, or something weaker.

meanings.short: A point where the fields of several charges cancel exactly, so the total field is zero and no field line passes through.
meanings.long: Between two equal charges of the same sign, for example, there is a null point halfway between them.

meanings.short: A molecule, such as water, whose charges are unevenly placed, so it is a small electric dipole even without an outside field.
meanings.long: In a polar molecule the centres of positive and negative charge do not coincide. A field turns polar molecules to line up with it, while heat keeps shaking them out of line. A non-polar molecule, such as methane, becomes a dipole only when a field stretches it.

meanings.short: How much of a field, or of a flow of matter or energy, passes through a surface (per second, for a flow).
meanings.long: The flux of a field through a surface adds up, over every small piece of the surface, the part of the field at right angles to it times the area. For a fluid's velocity field it is the volume crossing per second. Gauss's law and the divergence theorem are about the flux out of closed surfaces.

meanings.short: The energy of light arriving from a source per second through each square metre, sometimes per unit of frequency.
meanings.long: Astronomers call the measured brightness of a source its flux: the power received per unit area of detector. It falls with distance, unlike the surface brightness of an extended object.

meanings.short: The energy of light arriving from a source per second through each square metre.
A surface with no edge that completely encloses a region of space, like the skin of a ball.
meanings.long: A sphere or a cube is a closed surface; a flat disc or a hemisphere is open, with an edge. The flux out of a closed surface is measured with the normal pointing outwards.

meanings.short: A curve that ends where it started, like a circle, so it has no loose ends.
meanings.long: A loop drawn on paper or in space is a closed curve. Line integrals round closed curves measure circulation, and Green's and Stokes' theorems link them to what happens inside the curve.

meanings.short: How much a field or flow goes round a closed loop: the part of the field along the loop, added up all the way round.
meanings.long: The circulation is the line integral of the field round a closed curve. A fluid swirling in circles has circulation; Ampère's law says the circulation of the magnetic field equals μ₀ times the current through the loop. Circulation per unit area is measured by the curl.

meanings.short: The three-dimensional version of an angle: how much of the view around a point an object covers, measured in steradians.
meanings.long: A small area facing a point at distance r covers the solid angle area divided by r². The whole sphere of directions around a point is 4π steradians, just as a full turn is 2π radians.

meanings.short: The law that the flux out of any closed surface is set by what is inside: the charge for electric fields, the mass for gravity.
meanings.long: For the electric field the flux out equals the enclosed charge divided by ε₀; this form is one of Maxwell's equations. For gravity the flux of the gravitational field counts the mass inside. With a well-chosen surface, on which the field has the same size everywhere, it gives the field of symmetric charges (a sphere, a line, a plane) in a few lines.

meanings.short: An imaginary closed surface chosen to apply Gauss's law, usually shaped so that the field is the same everywhere on it.
meanings.long: To use Gauss's law one draws a closed surface, often a sphere, cylinder or pillbox matching the symmetry of the charges. It is a tool of the calculation, not a real object.

meanings.short: The electric potential energy a charge would have at a point, per coulomb of charge; measured in volts.
meanings.long: The potential V at a point is the work per unit charge needed to bring a test charge there from a reference point, usually far away. A charge q at the point has potential energy qV. The field points from high to low potential, along the steepest drop.

meanings.short: The gravitational potential energy a mass would have at a point, per kilogram of mass.
meanings.long: Near a mass M the gravitational potential is −GM/r. It plays the same role for gravity as the electric potential does for electric charges: the field points down its steepest slope.

meanings.short: A surface or line on which the electric potential is the same everywhere, so moving a charge along it takes no work.
meanings.long: Equipotentials are always at right angles to the field lines. Around a point charge they are spheres. A conductor in equilibrium is one equipotential.

meanings.short: The SI unit of electric potential and voltage: one joule of energy for each coulomb of charge.
meanings.long: A battery of 1.5 volts gives each coulomb passing through it 1.5 joules. Field strength can be given in volts per metre, the same as newtons per coulomb.

meanings.short: The difference in electric potential between two points, measured in volts: the energy each coulomb of charge gains or loses between them.
meanings.long: A battery keeps a voltage across its terminals; a current flows through a resistor because of the voltage across it. Only differences of potential can be measured, so voltage is always between two points.

meanings.short: A small unit of energy: the energy an electron gains moving through a voltage of one volt, about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ joules.
meanings.long: The electron volt (eV) is convenient for atoms and particles. Chemical bonds have a few eV; particle physics uses millions or billions of eV.

everyday: Not the person leading an orchestra or collecting fares: in physics a conductor is a material that carries charge.

meanings.short: A material in which electric charges can move freely, such as a metal, so that it carries current easily.
meanings.long: In a conductor some electrons are not bound to atoms. In electrostatic equilibrium they have arranged themselves so that the field inside the metal is zero and the whole conductor is at one potential.

meanings.short: A material, such as glass, rubber or plastic, in which charges cannot move freely, so it carries almost no current.
meanings.long: In an insulator every electron is bound to its atom or molecule. An electric field can still shift the charges slightly, which is why insulators placed between capacitor plates, called dielectrics, change the field.

meanings.short: The state of a conductor once its charges stop moving: the field inside the metal is zero and extra charge sits on the surface.
meanings.long: In equilibrium a conductor is one equipotential, and just outside it the field is at right angles to the surface. These facts follow from the fact that free charges keep moving as long as any field acts on them inside the metal.

meanings.short: A device that stores electric charge and energy, usually two metal plates held close together but not touching.
meanings.long: Charging a capacitor puts +Q on one plate and −Q on the other, with a voltage V between them. The ratio Q/V is its capacitance. The energy is stored in the electric field between the plates.

meanings.short: How much charge a capacitor stores for each volt across it, measured in farads.
meanings.long: Capacitance C is the charge Q on one plate divided by the voltage V between the plates. It depends only on the shape, size and spacing of the conductors and on the material between them, not on the charge.

meanings.short: An insulating material, such as glass or plastic, whose molecules an electric field lines up or stretches, weakening the field inside; used between capacitor plates.
meanings.long: Inside a dielectric the field polarizes the molecules, and the aligned dipoles partly cancel the field. For the same charge the voltage drops, so the capacitance rises by the dielectric constant.

meanings.short: The number by which a material between capacitor plates weakens the field and multiplies the capacitance: 1 for empty space, about 80 for water.
meanings.long: The dielectric constant κ is always at least 1: about 1.0006 for air, around 4 to 6 for glass. Filling a capacitor with the material multiplies its capacitance by κ.

meanings.short: The strongest electric field a material can stand before it breaks down and conducts, often with a spark.
meanings.long: For air the dielectric strength is about 3 million volts per metre. Above it, electrons are torn from molecules and the insulator suddenly conducts.

meanings.short: The current flowing through each square metre of a cross-section, as an arrow pointing along the flow of charge.
meanings.long: The current through a surface is the flux of the current density through it. If carriers of charge q, n of them per cubic metre, move with drift velocity v, the current density is nqv.

meanings.short: The slow average speed at which charges creep along a wire carrying a current, though each one moves fast and erratically.
meanings.long: Electrons in a metal move very fast in random directions, colliding with the atoms. A field adds a small average motion along the wire, the drift, typically far less than a millimetre per second.

meanings.short: How easily something flows through a material: electric current, for electrical conductivity, or heat, for thermal conductivity.
meanings.long: Electrical conductivity is the current density produced by each unit of electric field: in an ohmic material the current density is the conductivity times the field. Metals have a high conductivity, insulators a very low one, and it is one over the resistivity. Thermal conductivity likewise sets how fast heat flows for a given temperature difference.

meanings.short: How strongly a material resists the flow of current; one over its conductivity, measured in ohm metres.
meanings.long: A wire of length ℓ, cross-section area A and resistivity ρ has resistance ρℓ/A. Resistivity is a property of the material; resistance also depends on the object's shape.

meanings.short: How strongly something opposes an electric current: the voltage across it divided by the current through it, measured in ohms.
meanings.long: A resistor with resistance R carries current I = V/R when a voltage V is across it, and turns electrical energy into heat at the rate I²R.

meanings.short: How strongly something opposes an electric current: the voltage across it divided by the current through it, measured in ohms.
The SI unit of electrical resistance: one volt across it drives a current of one ampere.
meanings.long: Resistances in circuits range from fractions of an ohm for wires to millions of ohms for insulating parts.

meanings.short: Obeying Ohm's law: the current is proportional to the voltage, so the resistance stays the same whatever the voltage.
meanings.long: Metals at a fixed temperature are ohmic. Many devices are not: the resistance of a lamp filament rises as it heats up, and a diode lets current through one way only.

meanings.short: A circuit part made to have a chosen resistance, which limits the current and turns electrical energy into heat.
meanings.long: The voltage across a resistor is IR, in step with the current: in an alternating current circuit, unlike a capacitor or inductor, it absorbs energy on average.

meanings.short: The SI unit of electric current: one coulomb of charge passing a point each second.
meanings.long: The ampere, or amp, measures current. A phone charger delivers about one or two amperes; a lightning stroke tens of thousands.

everyday: Despite the name it is not a force but an energy per unit charge, measured in volts.

meanings.short: The energy a battery or other source gives each coulomb of charge it moves round a circuit; measured in volts, it is not a force.
meanings.long: A battery does work moving charge from its low to its high potential terminal; its emf is that work per unit charge. A changing magnetic flux also produces an emf, by Faraday's law.

meanings.short: The resistance inside a battery itself, which lowers the voltage at its terminals when it supplies a current.
meanings.long: A real battery acts like an ideal emf in series with a small resistor r. When it supplies a current I, the voltage at its terminals is the emf minus Ir.

meanings.short: Kirchhoff's rule that the total current flowing into any junction of a circuit equals the total flowing out.
meanings.long: Charge cannot pile up at a junction, so what flows in must flow out. Together with the loop rule it gives enough equations to find every current in a circuit.

meanings.short: Kirchhoff's rule that the voltage changes around any closed loop of a circuit add up to zero.
meanings.long: Going once round a loop and back to the start returns to the same potential. Adding the rises across batteries and the drops across resistors therefore gives zero.

meanings.short: Connected one after another in a single path, so the same current flows through each part.
meanings.long: Resistors in series add: the total resistance is their sum. Capacitors in series combine by adding the reciprocals of their capacitances.

meanings.short: Connected side by side between the same two points, so each part has the same voltage across it.
meanings.long: Capacitors in parallel add: the total capacitance is their sum. Resistors in parallel combine by adding the reciprocals of their resistances.

meanings.short: Two resistors in series across a voltage, so that the point between them gives a chosen fraction of that voltage.
meanings.long: With resistors R₁ and R₂ across V, the voltage across R₂ is V times R₂/(R₁ + R₂).

meanings.short: An instrument that measures electric current; it is placed in series with the part being measured and has a very small resistance.
An instrument that measures the voltage between two points; it is placed in parallel and has a very large resistance.
An instrument that measures resistance: it applies a small voltage across a part, measures the current that flows and divides.
meanings.long: An ohmmeter supplies its own voltage, so the part must be disconnected from any power source while it is measured.

meanings.short: A sensitive current meter: a coil on a spring in a magnet's field, which turns by an amount set by the current through it.
meanings.long: The current makes the coil a magnetic dipole, which the magnet's field twists against the spring. Ammeters and voltmeters were long built from galvanometers.

meanings.short: The force of electric and magnetic fields on a charged particle: a push along the electric field, plus a sideways magnetic push when it moves.
meanings.long: In symbols it is q(E + v × B). The magnetic part is at right angles to the velocity, so it bends the path of a charge without changing its speed. In a uniform magnetic field a charge moves in a circle or a helix.

meanings.short: The SI unit of magnetic field; one tesla is a strong field, about 20 000 times the Earth's field at its surface.
meanings.long: One tesla is one newton per ampere per metre: a wire carrying one ampere at right angles to a field of one tesla feels one newton per metre of length.

meanings.short: An older unit of magnetic field outside the SI: one gauss is 10⁻⁴ tesla, about twice the Earth's field at its surface.
One of the two ends of a magnet, north or south, where its field is strongest; like poles repel and unlike poles attract.
meanings.long: Cut a magnet in two and each piece has both poles again: no single magnetic pole has ever been found.

meanings.short: A small loop of current, or a small magnet, whose field far away has the same shape as that of an electric dipole.
meanings.long: A compass needle, a current loop and the electron are magnetic dipoles. In a field a magnetic dipole feels a torque that lines it up with the field, and in a non-uniform field a net force.

meanings.short: The strength and direction of a magnetic dipole: for a current loop, the current times the area, pointing along the loop's axis.
meanings.long: The torque on a dipole in a field B is the moment crossed with B, and its energy is minus the moment dotted with B, lowest when it points along the field.

meanings.short: The rule that gives the magnetic field made by each small piece of a current-carrying wire; adding the pieces gives the whole field.
meanings.long: Each piece of wire carrying current I contributes a field proportional to I and to the length of the piece, falling as one over distance squared, at right angles to both the wire and the line to the point.

meanings.short: The constant μ₀ that sets the strength of magnetic fields made by currents in empty space.
meanings.long: It appears in the Biot–Savart and Ampère laws. Together with the electric constant ε₀ it fixes the speed of light: c equals one over the square root of μ₀ε₀.

meanings.short: The law that the circulation of the magnetic field around any closed loop equals μ₀ times the current passing through the loop.
meanings.long: Like Gauss's law for the electric field, Ampère's law gives the field quickly when symmetry makes the field constant along a well-chosen loop: around a long wire, inside a solenoid or a toroid.

meanings.short: An imaginary closed loop chosen to apply Ampère's law, usually one along which the magnetic field is constant, or at right angles, or zero.
Ampère's law with Maxwell's addition: a changing electric field makes a magnetic field just as a current does.
meanings.long: The circulation of B around a loop equals μ₀ times the current through it plus μ₀ε₀ times the rate of change of the electric flux through it. Maxwell's extra term, the displacement current, is what allows electromagnetic waves.

meanings.short: Maxwell's extra term in Ampère's law: ε₀ times the rate of change of electric flux, which makes a magnetic field like a current does.
meanings.long: Between the plates of a charging capacitor no charge flows, yet a magnetic field circles the gap. The changing electric field there acts like a current, the displacement current, equal to the current in the wires.

meanings.short: A long coil of wire wound like a spring; a current through it makes a strong, nearly uniform magnetic field inside.
meanings.long: Inside a long solenoid with n turns per metre carrying current I the field is μ₀nI along the axis, and outside it is nearly zero.

meanings.short: A coil of wire wound round a ring shaped like a doughnut, which keeps its magnetic field inside the ring.
A pair of equal circular coils, one radius apart on a shared axis, which make a nearly uniform magnetic field between them.
Crossed electric and magnetic fields whose forces cancel for particles of one speed only, which pass straight through.
meanings.long: The electric force qE and the magnetic force qvB balance when v = E/B. Faster or slower particles are pushed aside.

meanings.short: An instrument that sorts charged particles by mass, by bending them in a magnetic field: heavier ones curve less.
meanings.long: Particles of known speed, often from a velocity selector, enter a magnetic field and move in circles whose radius gives their mass-to-charge ratio.

meanings.short: The magnetic dipole moment per unit volume of a material, from its atomic magnets lining up.
meanings.long: A magnetized material acts like a surface current running round it, which adds to or subtracts from the applied field.

meanings.short: A number saying how strongly a material becomes magnetized in a field: positive for paramagnets, small and negative for diamagnets.
meanings.long: In 8.02 the magnetization is χₘ times the applied field divided by μ₀, so the field inside is (1 + χₘ) times the applied one.

meanings.short: Of a material: weakly pushed out of a magnetic field, because the field makes its atoms set up a small opposing magnetization.
meanings.long: All materials are slightly diamagnetic; it shows only when nothing stronger hides it. A strong enough field can levitate a frog, which is mostly water.

meanings.short: Of a material: weakly pulled into a magnetic field, because the field partly lines up its atoms' own small magnets.
meanings.long: In a paramagnet the atomic dipoles point at random until a field turns them; heat keeps the alignment partial, and it disappears when the field is removed.

meanings.short: Of a material such as iron, called a ferromagnet: strongly magnetized by a field, because neighbouring atomic magnets line up together in regions called domains.
meanings.long: In a ferromagnet the field inside can be thousands of times the applied field, and part of the alignment survives when the field is removed. This is what makes permanent magnets.

meanings.short: A material, such as iron, whose atomic magnets tend to line up with their neighbours, so it can be magnetized without any outside field.
meanings.long: In the Ising model this is the case J > 0, where every pair of neighbouring spins prefers to be aligned. Above a critical temperature the alignment is lost and the material is no longer magnetic on its own.

meanings.short: The lagging of a system behind the changes acting on it, so its state depends on its past as well as on present conditions.
meanings.long: In a ferromagnet, turning the field up and then down again does not retrace the same magnetization: some remains at zero field, which is what makes permanent magnets. Each cycle round this loop turns some energy into heat. Other systems, such as one that jumps between two states as a setting is changed, show the same lag.

meanings.short: The amount of magnetic field passing through a surface: the field times the area, counting only the part of the field crossing it.
meanings.long: It is measured in webers. Faraday's law says a changing magnetic flux through a loop drives an emf around the loop, whether the field, the area or the angle changes.

meanings.short: The SI unit of magnetic flux: one tesla through one square metre.
meanings.long: A flux changing by one weber per second through a loop drives an emf of one volt around it.

meanings.short: The making of a voltage, and so a current, in a circuit by a changing magnetic field through it.
meanings.long: Discovered by Faraday in 1831, it is how generators, transformers and induction cookers work.

meanings.short: The law that a changing magnetic flux through a loop drives an emf around it, equal to minus the rate at which the flux changes.
meanings.long: The minus sign is Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change. Faraday's law also says that a changing magnetic field makes an electric field that circles round, which unlike an electrostatic field is not conservative.

meanings.short: The rule that an induced current always flows in the direction that opposes the change of magnetic flux that caused it.
meanings.long: If the flux through a loop rises, the induced current makes a field that pushes it back down; if it falls, the current tries to keep it up. This is the minus sign in Faraday's law, and it follows from conservation of energy.

meanings.short: A swirl of current set up inside a solid piece of metal by a changing magnetic field, which heats the metal and brakes its motion.
meanings.long: Eddy currents oppose the change that causes them, by Lenz's law. They are used in some brakes and cookers, and are reduced in transformers by building the core from thin insulated sheets.

meanings.short: A machine that turns motion into electricity, usually by spinning a coil in a magnetic field so the flux through it keeps changing.
meanings.long: The changing flux drives an alternating emf in the coil, by Faraday's law. A motor is the same machine run the other way.

meanings.short: A quantity that, applied again and again in tiny steps, builds up a whole transformation such as a shift, rotation or change of gauge.
meanings.long: In mechanics the momentum generates shifts in position, the angular momentum rotations and the Hamiltonian the motion in time. In general relativity a gauge generator is the small shift of coordinates that produces a change of gauge.

meanings.short: How strongly a coil opposes changes in the current through it: the magnetic flux it makes through itself per ampere, measured in henries.
meanings.long: A changing current I in a coil of self-inductance L produces the back emf −L dI/dt. A long solenoid has a large inductance because each turn's flux passes through all the others.

meanings.short: The magnetic flux a current in one coil sends through a second coil, per ampere; it sets the emf one coil induces in the other.
meanings.long: The mutual inductance is the same both ways: coil 1 in coil 2 gives the same value as coil 2 in coil 1. It depends only on the shapes, sizes and positions of the coils.

meanings.short: The SI unit of inductance: a one-henry coil has a back emf of one volt when its current changes by one ampere per second.
meanings.long: One henry is one volt second per ampere. Coils in electronics have inductances from microhenries to a few henries.

meanings.short: A coil of wire used in a circuit for its inductance: it resists changes of current and stores energy in its magnetic field.
meanings.long: An inductor behaves a little like mass in mechanics: it keeps a current flowing and opposes sudden changes. Its stored energy is half L I².

meanings.short: The emf an inductor produces when the current through it changes, pushing against that change.
meanings.long: When the current through a coil rises, its own changing flux induces an emf opposing the rise; when it falls, the emf tries to keep it going. It is also called the self-induced emf.

meanings.short: Two coils wound on a shared iron core, which raise or lower an alternating voltage in the ratio of their numbers of turns.
meanings.long: The alternating current in the first coil makes a changing flux that passes through the second, inducing a voltage there. Power lines carry electricity at high voltage and low current, to waste less as heat, and transformers step it down for homes.

meanings.short: Back-and-forth motion in which the push towards the middle is proportional to the distance from it, so the position follows a sine curve in time.
meanings.long: A mass on a spring, a small swing of a pendulum and the charge in an LC circuit all move this way. The period does not depend on the size of the swing.

meanings.short: Electric current that reverses direction many times a second, usually following a sine curve, as in mains electricity.
meanings.long: In Europe the mains alternates 50 times a second, in North America 60. Direct current, in contrast, flows one way only, as from a battery.

meanings.short: Alternating current: current that keeps reversing direction, or a voltage that keeps reversing sign, usually following a sine curve.
Direct current: current that flows steadily in one direction, as from a battery.
Short for direct current; in signal work, the constant part of a signal that does not oscillate, as in the all-ones DC vector.
meanings.long: Engineers borrow the name from steady direct current. The DC component of a signal is its average value, the part with zero frequency.

meanings.short: The frequency at which an outside force or voltage pushes on an oscillating system, which after a while oscillates at that frequency.
meanings.long: A driven system settles down to oscillate at the driving frequency, not at its own natural frequency. How large the response is depends on how close the two frequencies are.

meanings.short: The large response of an oscillating system when it is pushed at, or close to, its own natural frequency.
meanings.long: A swing pushed in time with its motion goes higher and higher. In a driven circuit the current is largest at resonance, when the reactances of the inductor and capacitor cancel. The less damping, the higher and narrower the peak.

meanings.short: In scattering, an energy at which a particle is briefly trapped near the target, so that it passes or scatters much more strongly there.
meanings.long: A resonance shows up as a sharp peak in the transmission or the cross-section as the energy is varied. The narrower the peak, the longer the particle stays trapped.

meanings.short: A number, written Q, saying how sharp a resonance is: the resonant frequency divided by the width of the peak.
meanings.long: A high quality factor means little damping: a tall, narrow resonance and an oscillation that dies away slowly. For a series RLC circuit Q = ω₀L/R.

meanings.short: A rotating arrow whose length is the amplitude of an oscillation; its shadow on one axis gives the value at each moment.
meanings.long: Phasors turn an alternating current problem into adding arrows: currents and voltages that peak at different times are arrows at different angles, and the angle between them is the phase difference.

meanings.short: In an alternating current circuit, the ratio of the voltage amplitude to the current amplitude: the combined opposition of resistance and reactances.
meanings.long: For a resistor, inductor and capacitor in series, the impedance is the square root of R² plus (X_L − X_C)². It depends on frequency and is smallest at resonance. It is measured in ohms.

meanings.short: How strongly a medium resists being set moving by a wave; for a string, the square root of tension times mass per unit length.
meanings.long: When a wave crosses from one string to another, how much is reflected and how much is transmitted depends only on the two impedances. Equal impedances give no reflection at all.

meanings.short: How strongly a capacitor opposes an alternating current: one over (angular frequency times capacitance), measured in ohms.
meanings.long: A capacitor blocks steady currents and lets fast oscillations through, so its reactance falls as the frequency rises. Its current leads the voltage by a quarter cycle.

meanings.short: How strongly an inductor opposes an alternating current: angular frequency times inductance, measured in ohms.
meanings.long: An inductor lets steady currents through and resists fast changes, so its reactance grows with frequency. Its current lags the voltage by a quarter cycle.

meanings.short: In an alternating current circuit, the cosine of the phase angle between current and voltage; it sets how much power is actually used.
meanings.long: The average power is the rms current times the rms voltage times the power factor. Only the resistor absorbs energy on average; the inductor and capacitor store it and give it back.

meanings.short: Root mean square: square the values, average them, then take the square root; for a sine wave it is the peak divided by √2.
meanings.long: The rms value of an alternating current or voltage is the steady value that would give the same average heating in a resistor. Mains voltages are quoted as rms values.

meanings.short: An antenna whose two rods are each a quarter of a wavelength long, so that it oscillates strongly at the frequency it is built for.
meanings.long: Charges sloshing up and down the rods radiate electromagnetic waves polarized along the antenna. The lesson notes that the same antenna is also called a half-wavelength antenna, after its total length.
